steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on an adaptive, lightweight MEMS-mirror LiDAR that decouples the sensor's viewpoint from the robot's pose so motion can be compensated in hardware during sensing. Motivate it with small fast robots, explain the key idea and the sensor, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation: sensors fixed to the robot; stabilization and active vision; why miniature robots can't rely on post-processing
2. Key idea: compensation during imaging (bio-inspired)
3. MEMS mirror-enabled adaptive LiDAR vs. PTZ cameras
4. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation
- autonomy driven by vision and depth sensors; implicit assumption: sensor pose w.r.t. robot fixed; viewpoint change needs robot pose change
- -> fast robots need motion compensation (camera-robot stabilization); robots must reorient to observe relevant scene parts
- stabilization and active vision: well-studied
- image stabilization example: mostly post-capture processing of sensor data
- not feasible for next-gen fast miniature robots: robotic bees, crawling/walking robots, micro-air vehicles
- RoboBee-type flapping-wing robots: high frequency rocking (about 120 Hz in one design), piezo-electric actuation
- wind affects micro-robots more than larger robots; aerodynamic instability from ornithopter-based shock absorption
- extreme egomotion of small robots -> any sensing hard
- software correction exists for cameras and LiDARs, but hard in real-time onboard (computation, energy, latency)
- without compensation for miniature devices, can't unlock one of the ten grand challenges in robotics

2. Key idea: compensation during imaging
- motion correction in sensor hardware during imaging; measurements already compensated, no onboard computing
- decoupling robot-camera geometry, controlling camera independent of robot pose -> new perspective on perception, simpler autonomy pipeline
- demo: MEMS-driven LiDAR, compensation two ways: (i) onboard IMU, (ii) external feedback of robot pose at high rate
- inspiration: animal eyes, fast mechanical movements compensating motion, real-time, high accuracy
- Fig. 2: frames V(t) of video of hawk (Buteo jamaicensis) moved by human trainer; average \sum_{t}\frac{V(t)}{T} over interval T -> blur except where the bird compensates

3. MEMS mirror-enabled adaptive LiDAR
- reorienting sensor pose useful in robotics, e.g. image alignment during motion in SLAM
- rigid attachment: camera gets all robot motion incl. jitter -> spurious features, localization errors, wrong feature association, inaccurate map
- our design: LiDAR image reorientation in hardware, no software processing
- PTZ cameras tried before; mechanical actuation reacts in ones of Hz -> not for real-time egomotion compensation; limited use on robots, most robots rigid sensors
- recent MEMS and opto-mechanical components; opto-MEMS very fast (many kHz); change LiDAR projection offset orientation during motion -> view effectively static
- two orders of magnitude (or more) faster than robot motion -> camera views independent of robot view
- compensation via onboard IMU or external feedback (motion tracking setup)
- robot focuses on control, camera does perception independently; planner needn't account for perception

- geometric characterization; hardware compensation reduces unknowns for proprioceptive and exteroceptive tasks; simulation of compensation delay and rate; Sec. III

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Modern autonomy is mostly driven by vision and depth sensors for perception. Most of these techniques implicitly assume that the relative pose of the sensor with respect to the robot is fixed, so changing the sensor viewpoint means changing the robot pose. This means that fast-moving robots have to deal with motion compensation (i.e. camera-robot stabilization), and that robots have to reorient themselves to observe the relevant parts of the scene. So stabilization and active vision are well-studied problems.

Let us take image stabilization as a specific example. Most of these methods are successful, but they compensate by post-capture processing of the sensor data. We argue that this is just not feasible for the next generation of fast miniature robots such as robotic bees, crawling and walking robots, and other micro-air vehicles. For example, flapping-wing robots like the RoboBee have a high frequency rocking motion (about 120 Hz in one design) because of the piezo-electric actuation. Environmental factors like wind affect micro-robots much more than a larger robot. Also there might be aerodynamic instability because of ornithopter-based shock absorption. The egomotion of small robots (and the sensors on them) is quite extreme, and this makes any sensing challenging. There are software methods that correct for these effects for cameras and LiDARs, but it is often hard to run them in real-time onboard because of the computational, energy and latency constraints on the robot mentioned above. If we don't have proper motion compensation for miniature devices, we will not be able to unlock the full potential of what is one of the ten grand challenges in robotics.

## Key Idea: Compensation during Imaging

Our idea is that motion correction should happen in the sensor hardware during imaging, so the measurements are already compensated and no onboard computing is needed. In this paper we show the motion compensation advantage of decoupling the robot-camera geometry. Being able to control the camera properties independently of the robot pose could bring a new perspective to robot perception and simplify the autonomy pipeline. We show this through the design of a MEMS-driven LiDAR, and we do compensation in two ways - (i) onboard IMU, and (ii) external feedback of the robot pose at a high rate.

We are inspired by animal eyes, which have fast mechanical movements that compensate for motion in real-time and with high accuracy. In Fig. 2 we show frames V(t) from a video of a hawk (Buteo jamaicensis) that is moved around by a human trainer. We also show the average of the video \sum_{t}\frac{V(t)}{T} over a time interval T. The averaged image is motion blurred, except where the hawk mechanically compensates for the shifts. We imagine biologically-inspired motion compensation that happens during sensing. These sensors need to change their orientation adaptively, in real-time, and together with robot goals like mapping or navigation. Basically, the rotation matrix R has to cancel out the robot motion to give a "stable" view of the scene.

## MEMS Mirror-enabled Adaptive LiDAR

- reorienting sensor pose: useful e.g. for image alignment during motion in SLAM; rigid attachment -> camera gets all robot motion incl. jitter -> spurious features, localization errors, wrong feature association, inaccurate map
- our sensor design: LiDAR image reorientation in hardware, no software processing
- PTZ cameras tried; mechanical actuation reacts in ones of Hz -> not for real-time egomotion compensation; most robots just have rigid sensors
- MEMS / opto-mechanical components, opto-MEMS fast (many kHz) -> change LiDAR projection offset orientation during motion, view effectively static
- two orders of magnitude (or more) faster than robot motion -> camera views independent of robot view
- compensation via onboard IMU or external feedback (motion tracking setup); robot focuses on control, planner needn't reason about perception
- MEMS LiDAR optics: small size, low power

Contributions:
- novel LiDAR sensor with MEMS mirror similar to existing LiDAR MEMS scanner; wide non-resonant scanning angles; IMU + external feedback; Fig. 1
- geometric characterization; fewer unknowns for proprioceptive/exteroceptive tasks; simulation of compensation delay and rate (Sec. III)
- compensation control algorithms; experiments and simulations (Sec. IV)
- UAV flight with proof-of-concept prototype; MEMS modulator tethered to heavy components (laser, photodetector, optics, driver circuit, signal processing circuitry); compensation in under 10 ms; video, Fig. 12
- Gazebo implementation; adapt LIO-SAM for motion compensation; open-sourced sensor, UAV sim environment, LIO-SAM adaptations

steps.text:

For example, flapping-wing robots like the RoboBee have a high frequency rocking motion (about 120 Hz in one design) because of the piezo-electric actuation. Environmental factors like wind affect micro-robots much more than a larger robot. Also there might be aerodynamic instability because of ornithopter-based shock absorption. The egomotion of small robots (and the sensors on them) is quite extreme, and this makes any sensing challenging. There are software methods that correct for these effects for cameras and LiDARs, but it is often hard to run them in real-time onboard because of the computational, energy and latency constraints on the robot mentioned above. If we don't have proper motion compensation for miniature devices, we will not be able to unlock the full potential of what is one of the ten grand challenges in robotics.

## Key Idea: Compensation during Imaging

Our idea is that motion correction should happen in the sensor hardware during imaging, so the measurements are already compensated and no onboard computing is needed. In this paper we show the motion compensation advantage of decoupling the robot-camera geometry. Being able to control the camera properties independently of the robot pose could bring a new perspective to robot perception and simplify the autonomy pipeline. We show this through the design of a MEMS-driven LiDAR, and we do compensation in two ways - (i) onboard IMU, and (ii) external feedback of the robot pose at a high rate.

We are inspired by animal eyes, which have fast mechanical movements that compensate for motion in real-time and with high accuracy. In Fig. 2 we show frames V(t) from a video of a hawk (Buteo jamaicensis) that is moved around by a human trainer. We also show the average of the video \sum_{t}\frac{V(t)}{T} over a time interval T. The averaged image is motion blurred, except where the hawk mechanically compensates for the shifts. We imagine biologically-inspired motion compensation that happens during sensing. These sensors need to change their orientation adaptively, in real-time, and together with robot goals like mapping or navigation. Basically, the rotation matrix R has to cancel out the robot motion to give a "stable" view of the scene.

## MEMS Mirror-enabled Adaptive LiDAR

Being able to reorient the sensor pose could have many uses in robotics, especially for image alignment during motion like in SLAM. If the camera and the robot are rigidly attached, the camera experiences all the motion of the robot, including jitter and other disturbances that are bad for the Visual SLAM task. This can cause spurious features, errors in localization, and incorrect feature association, which leads to an inaccurate map. In this paper we describe a sensor design that can do image reorientation of a LiDAR in hardware, without needing any software processing for the compensation. Before this, pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) cameras have tried to address this problem. But they use mechanical actuation that reacts in ones of Hz, so they are not suitable for tasks like real-time egomotion compensation. This is why PTZ cameras are used so little on robots - most robots just have their sensors rigidly attached.

Our designs get past these difficulties by using recently available microelectromechanical (MEMS) and opto-mechanical components to change camera parameters. Opto-MEMS components are known to be very fast (many kHz), and they let us change the LiDAR projection offset orientation while the robot moves, so the LiDAR view is effectively static. If we change the LiDAR views two orders of magnitude (or more) faster than the robot motion, the camera views can effectively be independent of the robot view. In this work we can compensate the LiDAR point cloud using an onboard IMU or external feedback such as a motion tracking setup. More generally, this kind of compensation lets the robot focus on the control task while the camera does perception (which the control task needs) independently. This greatly simplifies robot planning, because the planner does not need to account for perception and only needs to reason about the control task.

MEMS LiDAR optics have the advantages of small size and low power consumption. Beyond this, our algorithmic and system design contributions are:

- We present the design of a novel LiDAR sensor that uses a MEMS mirror similar to an existing LiDAR MEMS scanner. This design allows wide non-resonant scanning angles for arbitrary orientations. We integrate it with two types of feedback (IMU and external sensors) to show quick and high-rate motion compensation. Fig. 1 shows the design of our sensor.

- We describe and geometrically characterize our sensor, and show that compensation in hardware can reduce the number of unknowns for proprioceptive and exteroceptive tasks. In simulation, we characterize the effect of compensation delay and compensation rate to find the benefits for robot perception. The quantitative and qualitative results of these simulations are in Sec. III.

- We present the compensation control algorithms for our LiDAR. We also characterize how well compensation control performs through experiments and simulations in Sec. IV.

- We show UAV flight with a proof-of-concept hardware prototype that combines external feedback with the MEMS mirror for egomotion compensation. To make UAV flight possible, we tether the MEMS modulator to the other heavy components that are needed, like the laser, photodetector, optics, the driver circuit, and the signal processing circuitry. The mirror modulation and IMU measurement frequencies are much higher than typical robot egomotion. Our prototype MEMS compensated scan system can do this compensation in under 10 ms. Please see the accompanying video for the visualization, and see Fig. 12.

- We provide an implementation of the sensor in the Gazebo simulator. With this simulated sensor, we propose a framework to adapt a modern LiDAR SLAM pipeline to include motion compensation. We adapt the modern LiDAR SLAM pipeline LIO-SAM to use such a sensor with motion compensation and show how useful this motion compensation is. We have open-sourced the sensor implementation, the UAV simulation environment, and our LIO-SAM adaptations.

Modern autonomy is largely driven by vision and depth sensors for perception. Most such techniques implicitly assume that the relative pose of the sensor w.r.t. the robot is fixed, and that changes in sensor viewpoint require a change in the robot pose. This implies that fast-moving robots must deal with motion compensation (i.e. camera-robot stabilization) and that robots need to reorient themselves to observe the relevant parts of the scene. Correspondingly, stabilization [1,2,3,4] and active vision [5,6,7,8] are well-studied problems.

Consider the specific example of image stabilization. While successful, most such methods compensate through post-capture processing of sensor data. We contend that this is simply not feasible for the next generation of fast miniature robots such as robotic bees [9], crawling and walking robots [10], and other micro-air vehicles [11]. For example, flapping-wing robots such as the RoboBee exhibit a high frequency rocking motion (at about 120 Hz in one design) due to the piezo-electric actuation [12]. Environmental factors such as wind affect micro-robots to a greater extent than larger robots, and there might be aerodynamic instability due to ornithopter-based shock absorption [13]. The egomotion of small robots (and their onboard sensors) is quite extreme, making any sensing challenging. While there are software methods to correct for such effects for cameras [14] and LiDARs [15], these are often difficult to run in real-time onboard due to the computational, energy and latency constraints on the robot mentioned above. Without proper motion compensation for miniature devices, we will not be able to unlock the full potential of what is one of the ten grand challenges in robotics [16].

## I-A Key Idea: Compensation during Imaging

Our idea is for motion correction to happen in sensor hardware during imaging, so that measurements are already compensated without requiring onboard computing. This paper shows the motion compensation advantage of decoupling robot-camera geometry; providing the ability to control the camera properties independent of the robot pose could bring a new perspective to robot perception and simplify the autonomy pipeline. We demonstrate this through the design of a MEMS-driven LiDAR and perform compensation in two ways - (i) onboard IMU, and (ii) external feedback of robot pose at a high rate.

We are inspired by animal eyes, which have fast mechanical movements that compensate for motion in real-time and at high accuracy [17]. In Fig. 2, we show frames V(t) from a video of a hawk (Buteo jamaicensis) being moved by a human trainer [18]. We also show the average of the video \sum_{t}\frac{V(t)}{T} over a time interval T. Note that the averaged image shows motion blurring, except where the hawk mechanically compensates for the shifts. We envision biologically-inspired motion compensation that happens during sensing. Such sensors need to adaptively change their orientation in real-time and in concert with robot goals such as mapping or navigation. Effectively, the rotation matrix R must cancel out robot motion to provide a "stable" view of a scene.

## I-B MEMS Mirror-enabled Adaptive LIDAR

The ability to reorient sensor pose could have many uses in robotics, particularly in image alignment during motion such as in SLAM. If the camera and robot are rigidly attached, the camera experiences all the motion the robot experiences, including jitter and other disturbances that are detrimental to the Visual SLAM task. This could result in spurious features, errors in localization, and incorrect feature association, leading to an inaccurate map. In this paper, we describe a sensor design that can perform image reorientation of a LiDAR in hardware without the need for any software processing for such compensation. Previously, pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) cameras have attempted to address this problem. However, they use mechanical actuation which reacts in ones of Hz, making them unsuitable for tasks such as real-time egomotion compensation. This is evidenced by the limited use of PTZ cameras on robots - most robots simply have sensors rigidly attached.

Our designs break through these past difficulties by exploiting recently available microelectromechanical (MEMS) and opto-mechanical components for changing camera parameters. Opto-MEMS components are famously fast (many kHz), and they allow the LiDAR projection offset orientation to be changed during robot motion, so that the view of the LiDAR is effectively static. By changing LiDAR views two orders of magnitude (or more) faster than robot motion, we can effectively make camera views independent of the robot view. In this work, we compensate the LiDAR point cloud using an onboard IMU or external feedback such as a motion tracking setup. More generally, such compensation allows the robot to focus on the control task while the camera performs perception (which the control task requires) independently. This greatly simplifies robot planning, as the planner does not need to account for perception and only needs to reason about the control task at hand.

MEMS LiDAR optics have the advantages of small size and low power consumption [19,20,21]. Our algorithmic and system design contributions beyond this are:

- We present the design of a novel LiDAR sensor adopting a MEMS mirror similar to this LiDAR MEMS scanner [22]. This design enables wide non-resonant scanning angles for arbitrary orientations. We integrate it with two types of feedback (IMU and external sensors) to demonstrate quick, high-rate motion compensation. Fig. 1 shows the design of our sensor.

- We describe and geometrically characterize our sensor, showing that compensation in hardware can reduce the number of unknowns for proprioceptive and exteroceptive tasks. In simulation, we characterize the effect of compensation delay and compensation rate to identify benefits for robot perception. The quantitative and qualitative results of these simulations are shown in Sec. III.

- We present the compensation control algorithms for our LiDAR and further characterize the performance of compensation control through experiments and simulations in Sec. IV.

- We show UAV flight with a proof-of-concept hardware prototype combining external feedback with the MEMS mirror for egomotion compensation. We enable UAV flight by tethering the MEMS modulator to the other heavy necessary components, such as the laser, photodetector, optics, the driver circuit, and the signal processing circuitry. The frequencies of the mirror modulation and IMU measurement are much higher than typical robot egomotion, and our prototype MEMS compensated scan system can perform such compensation in under 10 ms. Please see the accompanying video for visualization, and see Fig. 12.

- We provide an implementation of the sensor in the Gazebo simulator. Using this simulated sensor, we propose a framework to adapt a modern LiDAR SLAM pipeline to incorporate motion compensation: we adapt LIO-SAM [23] to use such a sensor and demonstrate the utility of motion compensation. We have open-sourced the sensor implementation, the UAV simulation environment, and our LIO-SAM adaptations.
